title: The Perception of Visual Surfaces
research_question: To investigate whether the impression of slant of a visual surface is determined by the gradient of texture-density in the retinal image, in isolation from other depth cues.

participants.description: 10 paid observers (9 women, 1 man). Women included 3 students, 3 clerical workers, 3 psychology teachers. The man was an engineer.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Photographic images of wallpaper patterns (two types: 'regular' with rectangular elements, and 'irregular' with unfamiliar, unevenly distributed elements) projected as lantern-slides onto a translucent screen. These patterns were photographed at physical slants of 10°, 22°, 30°, and 45° from the perpendicular. Each slide was inverted to create upward and downward gradients of texture-density. Viewed monocularly through two hole-screens with head fixed.

measures.instrument: A 6-inch square composition-board, adjustable by the observer's right hand, rotated 90° backward or forward from a vertical plane. Observers adjusted the board until its tactual-kinesthetic impression matched the visual impression of slant.

findings.antecedent: Retinal gradient of texture-density (corresponding to physical slants of 10°, 22°, 30°, 45°)
findings.mechanism: The geometry of perspective dictates that a physical surface not perpendicular to the line of sight projects a texture distribution that gets denser as the surface recedes, and the gradient of density is proportional to the angle of slant. The visual system responds to this gradient.
findings.quote: The positive slopes of the lines joining the means actually obtained show that an increase in 'equivalent physical slant' is accompanied by an increase in the judged slant.

findings.mechanism: Regular texture consisted of repeating, adjacent, evenly-distributed elements with linear perspective, likely affording a more definite gradient of density and thus clearer predictions.
findings.quote: Apparently the regular texture yields a more definite impression of slant.

findings.antecedent: Experimental viewing conditions (visibility of projection screen texture, absence of differential blur, absence of accommodation cue, hole-screen slant, residual head-motion)
findings.mechanism: Conflicting cues from the setup (e.g., the projection screen's own texture, the frontal plane of the hole-screen) biased perceived slant towards a frontal surface, leading to a compromise judgment.

findings.antecedent: Correction for baseline discrepancy between objective vertical and tactual-kinesthetic vertical (mean 4.1° forward/ceilingwise)
findings.consequent: Apparent discrepancy between judged slant and physical slant equivalent for upward vs. downward density increase
findings.mechanism: The baseline for tactual-kinesthetic reproduction was not perfectly objective vertical for the setup, requiring a correction to accurately compare upward and downward gradient effects.
findings.quote: When this is done the discrepancy between the two curves disappears.

findings.consequent: Accuracy of slant judgments and degree of psychophysical correspondence with equivalent physical slant
findings.mechanism: Individual variability in how texture gradients are processed or how other cues/priors are weighted.
findings.quote: There were individual differences among Os which, of course, are not evident in the group-data.

findings.mechanism: Irregular texture functions less efficiently to determine slant, leading to more variable individual interpretations/predictions.
findings.quote: There were notably greater individual differences in the case of the irregular texture...

findings.antecedent: Opportunity to notice and remember size/shape relationships and modify judgments over time (main experiment)
findings.consequent: Use of inferences or 'cues' rather than immediate impressions
findings.mechanism: Observers might learn to employ ingenious techniques or use cues like size of elements, density of elements, or linear perspective to make judgments, potentially overriding initial automatic impressions.
findings.quote: Five Os mentioned that they deliberately used size of elements, density of elements, or linear perspective as cues...

findings.antecedent: Retinal gradient of texture-density (corresponding to physical slants of 10°, 22°, 30°, 45°), with single judgments per participant (preliminary experiment)
findings.mechanism: The gradient of density of the texture of a projected image is a fundamental stimulus for optical slant perception, even without opportunity for learning or inference.
findings.quote: When no opportunity for inferentially improving judgment was afforded, a psychophysical correspondence was obtained.

findings.antecedent: Differences in experimental setup (more visible projection screen texture, second hole-screen farther from O, adjustable board always pre-set at objective vertical) in preliminary experiment
findings.consequent: Slope of the curves (increase in judged slant for a given increase in physical slant equivalent)
findings.mechanism: Differences in the setup likely introduced conflicting cues or weakened the primary texture gradient cue, leading to a less pronounced effect on perceived slant.
findings.quote: There is evidence that the lesser slopes in this experiment are attributable to differences between the two set-ups.

mechanisms: The geometry of perspective dictates that a physical surface not perpendicular to the line of sight projects a distribution of texture-elements which gets denser as the surface recedes, and whose gradient of density is proportional to the angle of slant. The visual system responds to this gradient.
Regular texture provides a more definite gradient of density compared to irregular texture, leading to clearer perception.
Conflicting cues (e.g., projection screen's own texture, absence of differential blur, hole-screen's frontal slant, residual head-motion) can bias perceived slant towards a frontal plane.
moderators: Experimental setup details (e.g., visibility of projection screen texture, distance of hole-screen, opportunity for inference)
implementation_implications: The perspective of texture, as distinguished from the perspective of rectilinear outlines, seems to be a fundamental basis for the impression of a three-dimensional environment. This suggests that controlling texture gradients in visual displays or environments could be a powerful way to manipulate perceived depth and slant.

tables.description: Judged slant as a function of the gradient of texture density, recorded in degrees of tactual-kinesthetic inclination to the vertical, showing means of judgments by 10 Os and medians of their standard deviations.
key_stats: Mean judged slant values for 16 stimuli (texture type x physical slant equivalent x gradient direction)

limitations: The experimental setup, while designed to isolate the texture gradient cue, introduced other factors (e.g., visibility of the projection screen's own texture, absence of differential blur, hole-screen's frontal slant, residual head-motion) that favored the perception of a frontal surface, leading to a constant error.

The possibility that observers in the main experiment might have used inferences or learned cues over time, rather than relying solely on immediate impressions, was a concern (addressed by a preliminary experiment).
The 'irregular' texture was not precisely defined mathematically, making it hard to specify its exact properties.
The study focused only on 'optical slant' and not 'gravitational slant'.

paper_metadata.title: Can Humans Really Discriminate 1 Trillion Odors?
paper_metadata.crossref_title: On the dimensionality of odor space
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: There is great interest in understanding human olfactory experience from a principled and quantitative standpoint. The comparison is often made to color vision, where a solid framework with a three-dimensional perceptual space enabled a rigorous search for the underlying neural pathways, and the technological development of lifelike color display devices. A recent, highly publicized report claims that humans can discriminate at least 1 trillion odors, which exceeds by many orders of magnitude the known capabilities of color discrimination. This claim is wrong. I show that the failure lies in the mathematical method used to infer the size of odor space from a limited experimental sample. Further analysis focuses on establishing how many dimensions the perceptual odor space has. I explore the dimensionality of physical, neural, and perceptual spaces, drawing on results from bacteria to humans, and propose some experimental approaches to better estimate the number of discriminable odors.

environmental_features: Retinal texture gradients (corresponding to physical slants of 10°, 22°, 30°, 45°)
control_conditions: Conditions with isolated depth cues (e.g., texture-only, disparity-only)

theory_commitments.specific_claim: The visual system combines multiple depth cues (e.g., texture, binocular disparity) to estimate surface slant, and this integration can be described by models such as Bayesian optimal integration.

mechanism_chain.description: The visual system processes various retinal cues to construct a coherent perception of 3D surface properties like slant, often by integrating information from multiple sources.

steps.from_construct: Multiple initial slant estimates (e.g., from texture and disparity)

instruments_used.name: High-resolution display monitor
instruments_used.description: Used to present computer-generated visual stimuli to participants.

instruments_used.name: Custom psychophysical software
instruments_used.description: Software (e.g., MATLAB with Psychtoolbox) used to create and control stimulus presentation and record participant responses.

instruments_used.name: Response device
instruments_used.description: Input device (e.g., keyboard, mouse, joystick) used by participants to indicate their perceived slant.

stimulus_images.description: Examples of computer-generated textured surfaces with varying slants and texture types, illustrating texture gradients and binocular disparity.
